summary: Mobile calling and data, home internet, television and business connections, with African operations and the group’s tower-infrastructure business.
description: Airtel provides the networks and services that let customers make calls, use the internet and connect workplaces. For example, a household may buy a home-internet plan while a company pays to link its offices. Airtel must keep those connections working. Its group also includes African mobile and mobile-money operations and Indus Towers.
money: People and businesses pay for plans, connections and related services. The group also earns from telecom infrastructure. It pays for network equipment, power, maintenance, staff, customer support and rights to use radio frequencies, plus borrowing and other costs. A customer’s recharge is not all profit.
customers: Individual mobile users, households, organisations buying business connections, African mobile and mobile-money users, and telecom operators using tower sites. The customer and payment arrangement differ across these activities.
drivers: Paying customers, plan prices, customers leaving, service reliability, network and energy costs, further equipment spending and conditions in overseas countries.

groups.title: Mobile calling and internet
groups.examples: Prepaid and postpaid plans and mobile data.
groups.explanation: Prepaid users recharge before using the covered service; postpaid users pay under a billing arrangement. Airtel must provide the promised connection and capacity. More videos watched do not automatically mean more money paid.

groups.title: Home internet and television
groups.examples: Broadband, wireless home access where offered and digital TV.
groups.explanation: The household pays for a connection or subscription. Installing equipment, keeping the service working and providing support create costs beyond simply signing up the customer.

groups.title: Connections for organisations
groups.examples: Airtel Business connectivity and related services.
groups.explanation: For example, a business may need reliable links between workplaces. It pays for an agreed service, with requirements for installation, support and performance that differ from an individual phone plan.

groups.title: African services
groups.explanation: Mobile money lets users hold or move money through the service. Customer balances are not the same as Airtel’s earned fees. Local rules and currencies affect these businesses.

groups.title: Tower sites through Indus Towers
groups.examples: Towers, power and space for telecom equipment.
groups.explanation: Telecom operators need structures and sites on which to place equipment, with a power supply. Indus provides this physical support under customer arrangements. It is a different service from selling a phone plan.

basics.title: What has to exist before a phone can connect?
basics.text: The network needs radio-frequency rights, called spectrum, and equipment and fibre links that carry signals and data. The group must obtain permissions, install equipment and keep it working. A coverage map alone does not show how many paying customers use it.

steps.title: Arrange permissions, sites and equipment
steps.text: Obtain the required rights and build or use the network facilities needed to connect customers.

steps.title: Connect a paying customer
steps.text: Activate the plan, install a home connection or complete a business installation under the agreed terms.

steps.title: Keep the service usable
steps.text: Maintain equipment, power, enough capacity for traffic and customer support. Interruptions or poor service can cause customers to leave.

steps.title: Collect payments and fund the network
steps.text: Recharges, bills and contract payments must cover service costs and other obligations. Equipment upgrades and further network construction need cash as well.

specifics.title: Average customer spending is not every customer’s bill
specifics.text: ARPU means average revenue per user under the company’s stated definition. It can change because prices rise or because a different set of customers and plans is included. Check the country and business covered.

specifics.title: An operating earnings measure leaves costs still to pay
specifics.text: EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax and the accounting charges for equipment and other assets losing value over time. It is not money left after buying equipment, paying for spectrum or meeting all borrowing and lease obligations.

specifics.title: The group includes more than India phone plans
specifics.text: African currencies can change the rupee value of results. Tower services and mobile money also earn differently from phone plans. Compare the same businesses and ownership arrangements across periods.

watch: A subscriber count alone cannot show a useful customer relationship.
Read active-user definitions, customer additions and customers leaving, alongside average spending and service quality. Compare the same business and country.
Higher plan prices and different customers can both change the average.
Read price changes, prepaid and postpaid plans, and the ARPU definition. Separate more paying users from more revenue per user.
Does network spending serve actual customer needs?
Equipment installed is different from customers paying to use it.
Read spending, service quality and actual connection use together. Check the payment dates for spectrum, equipment and leased sites rather than treating operating earnings as spare cash.
Do home and business connections cover their costs?
Installation and support can require money before payments arrive.
Compare paying connections with homes the network could reach. For business customers, read sales, promised support and bills still unpaid.
Which countries and companies does the comparison include?
Currency and ownership changes can alter group totals.
Compare local-currency and rupee results and check when companies enter group accounts. Keep Airtel Africa, India mobile and whole-group measures distinct.
risks: Customers switch or prices come under pressure
Competing plans can make it harder to keep customers without discounts or extra spending.
Spectrum, equipment upgrades and leased sites can require payments even while the business reports profit.
Outages, security problems and breaches of licence conditions can interrupt service and damage trust.
Currency movements, inflation and local rules can change costs and reported results.
context: One postpaid bill can pay for several services

Airtel’s 7 October 2026 release describes new postpaid plans, where the customer pays a monthly bill rather than recharging in advance. They combine unlimited calls and data, spam and fraud protection, subscriptions to other companies’ entertainment and storage apps and, from 8 October 2026, one free international-roaming pack per SIM each year. Roaming means using the phone on networks abroad. One bill therefore covers Airtel’s own network service as well as items supplied by other companies or used abroad. The release does not say what Airtel pays for those items, so the plan price is not all Airtel’s to keep. Keeping a household longer helps only if the payments cover these costs.
quiz: Is EBITDA the cash left after paying for all network expansion?
No. It leaves important costs and cash payments outside the measure. Check equipment spending, spectrum, leases, borrowing and tax separately.

financialNotes.title: Match service, country and measurement basis
financialNotes.text: The table preserves the audited segment definitions and separates segment sums from consolidated revenue after internal-sales eliminations. The reported earnings measure comes before financing, exceptional items and tax. Do not combine India customer-spending averages, Africa revenue and a group EBITDA margin into an invented profit calculation.
